assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the working core of modern monetary policy analysis. Calvo's time-dependent pricing, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's microfounded framework for monetary policy are used daily in central banks. The work shaped both theory and policy practice.
assessment.attribution: The field is crowded: Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler also made major contributions, and Clarida-Gali-Gertler and Smets-Wouters are not fully captured by a three-person cut. The three chosen names correspond to the foundational pricing mechanism, the policy rule and the integrated normative framework. A three-person limit necessarily omits important contributors.
assessment.maturity: The ideas date from the 1970s to the early 2000s and have decades of use and critique, including through the financial crisis and the post-2021 inflation episode. No further confirmation is needed.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer a different triad, such as one including Gali or Christiano and Eichenbaum.
The 2022 prize already recognised related banking and macro-finance work.
Empirical performance of the framework during the 2021-23 inflation is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Heterogeneous-firm trade models changed how trade is analysed. They explain exporter selection, intra-industry reallocation and gains from trade beyond comparative advantage. The framework spawned a very large empirical and quantitative literature and informs trade policy evaluation.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central theoretical contribution, with Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) on exports versus FDI. Helpman has a long record of foundational trade theory. Redding is an important contributor but later, and Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are also relevant and not credited here.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of citations, extensive empirical validation and integration into quantitative trade models mean the contribution is well established.
uncertainties: Omitted credit to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and to Redding.
Trade was recognised in 2008 for the New Trade Theory, so the committee may weigh field balance.
Helpman's other work, including with Grossman on trade politics, may be seen as a separate contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's 'Credit Cycles' (1997) showed how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks. It is the foundation of the modern macro-finance literature on balance-sheet channels and financial crises. It is widely used in post-2008 policy and research.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist are important in the financial accelerator and its empirical side, but the 2022 prize covered adjacent banking and crisis work by Bernanke. I therefore limit the proposal to the two originators.
assessment.maturity: Nearly thirty years since publication, with extensive follow-up and use in policy models. The credit-cycle mechanism has been confirmed in many studies.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises.
Whether the committee would include Gertler for the financial accelerator.
Moore's contributions in contract theory may or may not factor in.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model (1982) gave a tractable, strategic foundation for bargaining. It underlies models in labour, trade, macro and market design. It is one of the most widely applied results in game theory.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein's 1982 paper is the central contribution. Wolinsky (market bargaining, with Rubinstein) and Binmore (the Nash-programme link and the relation to Stahl) are important but secondary. A single laureate is the cleanest attribution.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years of use and theoretical extension. Well established.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to add Wolinsky or Binmore.
Game theory has been recognised often (1994, 2005, 2007, 2012, 2020), so there may be a field-balance concern.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Long-run series on top income and wealth shares transformed the empirical study of inequality and public debate. They also opened a data-driven research programme in public economics and macro. Impact on both scholarship and policy discussion is large.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the top-income series, with Zucman adding offshore wealth and distributional national accounts. The conceptual contribution is partly data construction. Piketty's theoretical claims about r > g are contested, while the measurement contribution is stronger.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work dates to the early 2000s and is well replicated and extended. The interpretation of long-run dynamics is still debated.
uncertainties: Debate about measurement methodology, especially for wealth and distributional accounts.
Whether the committee values data construction as a Nobel-level contribution.
Whether Zucman should be included given his career stage.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Persson, Tabellini and Besley built the modern theory and empirics of how political institutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. They carried political economics into mainstream applied economics. The contribution is substantial and has grown steadily.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini, partly through their 2000 book, are the core pair, and Besley is a major figure on state capacity and accountability. The 2024 prize recognised related institutions-and-growth work by Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson, which complicates field balance.
assessment.maturity: Work over three decades, with strong empirical support from constitutional and electoral-rule studies.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity.
Persson is a past committee member, which is disclosed here, not adjudicated, and which the committee would need to handle.
Whether the committee sees this as a distinct contribution from earlier prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data provided credible, geographically detailed measurement of intergenerational mobility and neighbourhood effects. It changed how mobility is studied and fed directly into policy design. The empirical contribution is important and influential.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads the programme; Hendren is central to the neighbourhood-effects and mobility work. Friedman and Katz are significant co-authors. Credit is spread across a large team, which makes a three-person limit difficult.
assessment.maturity: The main results are from 2014 onwards, and some replication and follow-up exists. A programme this recent has had less time for long-run testing.
uncertainties: Relatively recent work and an ongoing programme.
Team-based credit, where allocation is hard.
Chetty has other major contributions, for example in public economics, that could be weighed, but those are not part of this ballot entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance literature established the link between legal origins, investor protection and financial development, and launched a large body of cross-country comparative work. It influenced corporate governance and development policy.
assessment.attribution: Shleifer is central, working with La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes and Vishny on legal origins and investor protection. Vishny's role in the earlier corporate-finance work overlaps with these names. Credit is clearly shared among the four.
assessment.maturity: Work from the late 1990s with extensive follow-up, though the legal-origins thesis has been substantially criticised on identification and measurement grounds.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of legal-origins identification and the rights indices.
A three-person limit omits Vishny.
Professional controversies around individual candidates are not assessed here beyond noting their existence.
